screens.title: Auditing and Governance with AWS CloudTrail and AWS Config
screens.narratorSegment: In cloud operations, being able to answer who did what, and how resources changed, is essential for security and compliance. In this chapter you will learn the distinct but complementary roles of two AWS services: CloudTrail, which records A P I activity across your account, and AWS Config, which records what your resources look like and how they change over time. You will see practical configuration steps to enable CloudTrail across all regions, deliver logs to an S3 bucket and CloudWatch Logs, and create alerts for important events. You will also learn how AWS Config captures configuration items, evaluates resources against managed or custom Config Rules, and reports non-compliance so you can automate remediation. These capabilities together give you an audit trail for investigations and a continuous compliance posture for governance. As you work through the hands-on scenario, focus on the practical trade-offs: CloudTrail gives forensic detail about actions, while Config gives the history of resource state. By the end, you should be able to choose which service to use for a given governance goal and design a logging and compliance baseline that reduces manual review and speeds incident response. Which question would you ask first when designing an audit plan?

screens.title: CloudTrail vs AWS Config — A Practical Contrast
screens.narratorSegment: Let's clarify the core difference between AWS CloudTrail and AWS Config using practical questions you might ask. If you need to know who called the A P I to create an EC2 instance, which A P I operation ran, and when it occurred, CloudTrail is the service that answers that question. CloudTrail records A P I calls made by users, roles, or AWS services, and delivers those events to S3 and optionally to CloudWatch Logs for real-time monitoring. By contrast, if you need to know whether an S3 bucket is currently publicly accessible or what its configuration was last week, AWS Config answers that. Config captures configuration items — snapshots of resource settings — and stores a history you can query. A useful mental model is: CloudTrail tells you what happened; Config tells you what things look like and how they changed. A common misconception is thinking Config replaces CloudTrail; it does not. They are complementary: CloudTrail helps with forensic timelines and who-did-what; Config helps you detect drift from desired configuration and assess compliance. For example, if an S3 bucket's policy changed and a public object appears, CloudTrail shows which A P I call modified the policy and who made it, while Config shows the resulting public configuration and flags the bucket as non-compliant if you have a rule for public-read. The takeaway is to design logging and compliance together: enable CloudTrail for events you care about and use Config Rules to continuously evaluate the resource state you must enforce. Which question will you ask first in your next incident review?

keyIdea.title: Complementary Roles
keyIdea.text: Use CloudTrail for API-level audit trails and AWS Config for resource state history and continuous compliance.

content.html:
Core Concept
CloudTrail
Audit trail of API calls made by users, roles, and services.
Primary use

Forensic analysis, security investigations, and logging API activity to S3 and CloudWatch Logs.

  • Records who performed actions and when.
  • Can capture management events and optional data events.
  • Integrates with CloudWatch Logs for alarms.
Common Mistake

Not enabling management events or forgetting data events when deep visibility is required.

Core Concept
AWS Config
Continuous recording of resource configurations and compliance evaluation.
Primary use

Track resource configuration history, evaluate rules, and flag non-compliant resources.

  • Captures Configuration Items representing resource state at a point in time.
  • Uses managed or custom rules to assess compliance continuously.
  • Can trigger remediation actions when non-compliance is detected.
Key Takeaway

Use Config to enforce desired state and CloudTrail to answer who initiated changes.

screens.title: AWS CloudTrail Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: AWS CloudTrail is essentially an audit log for your AWS account. It records A P I calls and related events made by users, roles, or AWS services, creating a timeline of actions you can use for security analysis, troubleshooting, and compliance. Practically, enabling CloudTrail means you will receive event files in an S3 bucket and can optionally forward those events to CloudWatch Logs to build alerts. A best practice is to enable a multi-region trail so you capture events across all regions and to store logs in a dedicated, tightly controlled S3 bucket — ideally in a separate logging account — to reduce the risk of tampering during an incident. CloudTrail distinguishes management events and data events: management events capture control plane operations like creating or deleting resources, while data events capture resource-level operations such as S3 object A P I calls or Lambda invocation records. A common decision point is whether to enable data events, because they can be high volume and increase cost. You should choose data events selectively for critical resources where object-level visibility matters. For example, enabling S3 data events for a bucket that contains sensitive data helps detect unauthorized object reads. A misconception to avoid is relying on CloudTrail alone for compliance: CloudTrail shows actions, but it does not assess whether your resources are configured correctly—use Config for that. How would you choose which S3 buckets to include as data events in your account?

keyIdea.title: CloudTrail records API activity
keyIdea.text: Enable multi-region trails, deliver logs to a secure S3 bucket, and selectively enable data events for deep visibility.

content.html:
Definition
AWS CloudTrail
An audit trail of API calls for security, troubleshooting, and compliance.
Core behavior

Records management and optional data events, writing logs to S3 and optionally CloudWatch Logs for alarms.

  • Management events: control plane operations like CreateBucket or RunInstances.
  • Data events: resource operations like GetObject or Invoke — higher volume and greater detail.
  • Best practice: store logs in a dedicated, secured S3 bucket and enable multi-region trails.
Pro Tip

Enable CloudTrail in all regions and protect the log bucket with restricted access and versioning where appropriate.

Example: When to enable S3 data events
{ $.eventName = "GetObject" }
If a bucket stores sensitive documents, enable data events for object-level logging to detect reads and potential data exfiltration. Remember that data events can increase log volume and cost, so apply them selectively.
Key Takeaway

CloudTrail provides a reliable record of who performed which API actions and when. Use Config to judge whether the resulting configuration complies with policy.

screens.title: Delivering CloudTrail Logs and Creating Alerts
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through the process of creating a CloudTrail trail that writes to an S3 logging bucket and to CloudWatch Logs so you can create alerts. Start by creating a new trail and select the option to apply it to all regions. When you create the trail, choose or create a dedicated S3 bucket for logs. Protect that bucket with restrictive ACLs and consider placing it in a separate logging account to reduce tampering risk. Next, enable the CloudWatch Logs integration and create a log group for the trail. With events streaming into CloudWatch Logs you can create a metric filter that looks for root user activity or other critical events, and then create an alarm that publishes to an SNS topic. The chapter provides a filter pattern you can use to detect root activity. A common pitfall is forgetting to enable management events or misunderstanding data events: management events are essential for control plane visibility, while data events are optional and should be enabled for high-value resources only. In practice, enable a baseline of management events for all resources, forward to CloudWatch Logs for rapid detection, and add data events selectively where needed. When you create the alarm, test by triggering a benign root-level event in a controlled environment and confirm the SNS notification. What specific event would you choose to validate your alarm without creating risk?

keyIdea.title: Trail → S3 → CloudWatch
keyIdea.text: Create a multi-region trail, secure the S3 bucket, forward events to CloudWatch Logs, and create metric filters and alarms.

content.html:
Process Flow
Configure Trail and Alerts
A step-by-step flow from trail creation to alarm testing.
  1. 1. Create CloudTrail named MyOrganizationTrail and select "Apply trail to all regions."
  2. 2. Create a dedicated S3 bucket for logs and restrict access; consider a separate logging account.
  3. 3. Enable send CloudTrail events to CloudWatch Logs and create a log group.
  4. 4. Create a CloudWatch Metric Filter for root user activity and an Alarm that publishes to SNS.
  5. 5. Test the alarm in a sandbox and validate SNS delivery.
Common Mistake

Not protecting the log bucket or placing logs in the same account as the resources increases risk of log tampering.

Metric Filter Example
{ $.userIdentity.type = "Root" && $.userIdentity.userName = "root" && $.eventType != "AwsServiceEvent" }
Use this filter to count root user events. Create a metric from the filter and alarm when the count is greater or equal to 1 over a short window.
Key Takeaway

Forwarding CloudTrail to CloudWatch Logs enables real-time detection and alerts for critical events like root activity.

screens.title: AWS Config — Configuration Items and Continuous Recording
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Config continuously monitors and records configuration changes for supported AWS resources. Every time a supported resource changes, Config captures a Configuration Item — a snapshot of that resource's settings at a point in time. This recorded history lets you answer questions like what a security group's inbound rules looked like yesterday, or whether an EC2 instance's tag changed before a deployment failure. Config can be set to record all resources or only selected resource types; it delivers snapshots and a configuration history to an S3 bucket and sends notifications to an SNS topic. A practical benefit is troubleshooting: when an application breaks, use Config to find recent configuration changes that could explain the behavior. Importantly, Config is not an event log of who called an A P I; it records the resulting resource configuration. A common misconception is to rely on Config alone for auditing A P I activity — it will tell you that a configuration changed, but CloudTrail tells you who made the A P I call that caused it. When enabling Config, create an IAM role for Config if prompted, and plan a bucket for snapshots and history. The core insight is that Config gives you the state and history needed to detect drift and measure compliance over time. How would you use configuration history to accelerate a post-incident review?

keyIdea.title: Configuration Items
keyIdea.text: Config captures snapshots of resource settings over time so you can review history, detect drift, and support audits.

content.html:
Definition
AWS Config and Configuration Items
Record what resources look like and how they change, for continuous audit and troubleshooting.
What a Configuration Item contains
  • Resource type and identifier.
  • Configuration details at the capture time.
  • Relationships to other resources and a timestamp.
Recording options

Record all resources for broad coverage, or choose specific resource types to limit cost and noise. Configure an S3 bucket for history and an SNS topic for notifications.

Misconception

Config is not a substitute for CloudTrail. Use Config for state and CloudTrail for who-did-what.

Key Takeaway

Config gives you a historical record of resource configurations so you can detect drift, audit settings, and support automated compliance workflows.

screens.title: AWS Config Rules and Automated Compliance
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Config Rules let you evaluate whether resources meet your desired configuration. Rules can be managed (predefined) or custom. A managed rule example mentioned in the chapter is s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited, which flags S3 buckets that allow public read access. Another common managed rule is required-tags, which checks whether specific keys like Environment exist on resources such as EC2 instances. When you add a rule, Config continuously evaluates resources and marks them as compliant or non-compliant. For non-compliant resources you can trigger remediation, for example by invoking AWS Systems Manager Automation documents or other automated workflows. This moves governance from periodic audits to continuous enforcement. A practical implementation pattern is to align Config Rules with organizational policy and regulatory frameworks so compliance reporting is automated. Be mindful of rule scope and parameters: set required-tags with a Tag1Key parameter equal to Environment when that is your policy. A typical misconception is expecting immediate results; Config evaluations run on a schedule and may take a few minutes to appear. In practice, test rules in a non-production account and tune their scope to reduce noise. The closing question is: which rule would you enable first to reduce your organization's highest compliance risk?

keyIdea.title: Config Rules
keyIdea.text: Rules evaluate resource state continuously and can trigger remediation to enforce policy automatically.

content.html:
Process Flow
Implement Config Rules
Select rules, set parameters, evaluate compliance, and optionally automate remediation.
Managed Rule: s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited

Automatically flags buckets that allow public reads, a common source of data exposure.

Managed Rule: required-tags

Use parameters to require tags such as Environment. Resources without the tag are non-compliant.

Automated Remediation

When non-compliant, trigger SSM Automation or other actions to remediate or notify owners.

Why this matters

Rules let you demonstrate continuous compliance and reduce manual audits by surfacing non-compliant resources automatically.

Misconception

Expect a short evaluation delay after enabling a rule — evaluations are not always instant.

screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough summarizes the hands-on steps you will perform in the console. keyIdea.title: Hands-on Steps
keyIdea.text: Create MyOrganizationTrail, a secured S3 bucket, forward events to CloudWatch, and create a metric filter plus alarm for root activity.

content.html:
Hands-on
Enable CloudTrail and Alarm
Console steps summarized with the metric filter for root activity.
Console Steps
  1. Create CloudTrail: Name MyOrganizationTrail, apply to all regions.
  2. Create an S3 bucket for logs and restrict access; enable bucket versioning if desired.
  3. Enable CloudWatch Logs integration and create a log group.
  4. Create a CloudWatch Metric Filter and then an Alarm that publishes to an SNS topic.
Metric Filter (use in CloudWatch)
{ $.userIdentity.type = "Root" && $.userIdentity.userName = "root" && $.eventType != "AwsServiceEvent" }
Create a metric from this filter and alarm when the count is greater or equal to 1 in a short period to detect root activity.
Key Takeaway

Forwarding CloudTrail to CloudWatch Logs gives you the real-time signal needed to detect and act on suspicious API calls.

screens.title: Hands-on: Enable AWS Config and Add Rules
screens.narratorSegment: In this activity you will enable AWS Config to record resource configurations and add rules that evaluate compliance. Start by choosing Get started in the AWS Config console and select Record all resources unless you prefer a scoped approach. Provide an S3 bucket for Config snapshots and history and create an SNS topic for notifications. If prompted, create the required IAM role for AWS Config to read resource configurations. After Config is recording, add Config Rules. Search for s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited and add it; this managed rule flags any bucket that allows public read access. Next, add the required-tags rule and set the Tag1Key parameter to Environment so Config evaluates EC2 instances and other resources for that tag. When a resource is non-compliant, Config shows it in the console and can trigger notifications or remediation workflows. A common operational detail is to test rules in a non-production account to tune parameters and reduce false positives. Use the Config dashboard to review compliance history and export reports for audits. The immediate benefit is continuous assessment: instead of periodic checks, your environment is evaluated continuously and you get early warning of drift. What rule would you enable first to reduce your team's most frequent misconfiguration?

narration.text: In this activity you will enable AWS Config to record resource configurations and add rules that evaluate compliance. Start by choosing Get started in the AWS Config console and select Record all resources unless you prefer a scoped approach. Provide an S3 bucket for Config snapshots and history and create an SNS topic for notifications. If prompted, create the required IAM role for AWS Config to read resource configurations. After Config is recording, add Config Rules. Search for s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited and add it; this managed rule flags any bucket that allows public read access. Next, add the required-tags rule and set the Tag1Key parameter to Environment so Config evaluates EC2 instances and other resources for that tag. When a resource is non-compliant, Config shows it in the console and can trigger notifications or remediation workflows. A common operational detail is to test rules in a non-production account to tune parameters and reduce false positives. Use the Config dashboard to review compliance history and export reports for audits. The immediate benefit is continuous assessment: instead of periodic checks, your environment is evaluated continuously and you get early warning of drift. What rule would you enable first to reduce your team's most frequent misconfiguration?

keyIdea.title: Enable & Rule
keyIdea.text: Turn on Config recording, store snapshots, and apply managed rules like s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited and required-tags.

content.html:
Hands-on
Enable AWS Config and Add Rules
Record resources, provide an S3 bucket, and add managed rules for continuous compliance.
Setup steps
  1. Open AWS Config, choose Get started, and select Record all resources or specific types.
  2. Create an S3 bucket for Config snapshots and a new SNS topic for notifications.
  3. Create an IAM role for Config if requested and enable recording.
Add Rules
  1. Add s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited to flag public buckets.
  2. Add required-tags and set Tag1Key to Environment to require that tag on EC2 instances.
  3. Review compliance results and configure remediation as needed.
Key Takeaway

Config Rules let you codify policy and get continuous reports on compliance, reducing manual checks and improving governance.

screens.title: Testing Compliance — S3 and EC2 Examples
screens.narratorSegment: Testing your rules is essential to ensure Config evaluates resources as you expect. The chapter provides two concrete tests. First, create an S3 bucket and deliberately disable Block all public access or make an object publicly readable. Wait a few minutes and then check the s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited rule in Config; it should display the bucket as non-compliant. Fix the bucket by re-enabling Block all public access and observe the rule return to compliant. Second, launch an EC2 instance without the Environment tag and wait for the required-tags rule to evaluate; it should show non-compliant for that instance. Add the Environment tag and watch the resource become compliant. These tests demonstrate how Config surfaces non-compliance and helps you validate remediation. A typical misconception is expecting immediate results; allow Config time to evaluate and consider event timing. Also, ensure your Config recording covers the resource types you are testing. Use the Config console to view compliance timelines and to export a compliance report for audits. Testing in a sandbox account helps tune rule parameters and reduce false positives before deployment to production. After testing, think about automating remediation for common findings — what would you automate first?

keyIdea.title: Test & Observe
keyIdea.text: Deliberately create non-compliant S3 and EC2 resources to validate Config Rules and remediation processes.

content.html:
Testing & Validation
S3 and EC2 Compliance Tests
Create non-compliant resources and confirm Config flags them and updates status after remediation.
S3 Public Test
  1. Create an S3 bucket and disable Block all public access or make an object public.
  2. Wait a few minutes and check s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited in AWS Config for non-compliance.
  3. Fix the bucket and observe the rule return to compliant.
EC2 Tagging Test
  1. Launch an EC2 instance without the Environment tag.
  2. Check the required-tags rule; the instance should be non-compliant.
  3. Add the tag and confirm the resource becomes compliant after evaluation.
Misconception

Expect a short delay for evaluations; rules are not always instantaneous. Plan tests accordingly.

screens.title: Governance Best Practices and Deployment Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: When building an auditing and governance architecture, apply a few repeatable best practices. First, centralize logs and configuration history where possible: send CloudTrail logs and AWS Config snapshots to S3 buckets that are hardened and, when appropriate, owned by a separate logging account. This reduces risk during investigations and makes access control simpler. Second, enable CloudTrail as a multi-region trail so you capture activity regardless of region. Third, thoughtfully enable data events only for high-value resources due to cost and volume considerations. Fourth, align AWS Config Rules with organizational policies and compliance frameworks such as PCI or HIPAA, selecting managed rules where they match and creating custom rules for organization-specific checks. Fifth, integrate CloudTrail to CloudWatch Logs for real-time alerting on critical events and use SNS for notifications. Finally, plan remediation: Config can trigger remediation via Systems Manager Automation or other mechanisms. A common operational pitfall is scattering logs across many buckets and accounts without consistent policies; centralization and strong bucket protection avoid that. The overall insight is to design for both forensic capability and continuous enforcement so that audits become mostly automated and investigations faster. What single change could you make this week to better protect your audit trail?

keyIdea.title: Best Practices
keyIdea.text: Centralize logs, use multi-region trails, limit data events selectively, align rules to policy, and automate remediation where possible.

content.html:
Architecture
Governance Patterns
Design your logging and compliance layers to be centralized, protected, and automated.
Centralized Logs

Use a dedicated logging account and protected S3 buckets for CloudTrail and Config history to avoid tampering.

Multi-region Trails

Enable CloudTrail across all regions to ensure full coverage and consistent forensic data.

Selective Data Events

Enable data events only for critical high-value resources to balance visibility and cost.

Automate

Use Config Rules plus remediation to reduce manual fixes and maintain a steady compliance posture.

Operational Caution

Avoid scattering logs and inconsistent policies; centralization and strict access control are critical.

screens.title: When to Use CloudTrail, Config, or Both
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding which service to use depends on the question you need answered. Use CloudTrail when you need an audit trail of A P I activity — for example, to discover which principal called DeleteBucket or RunInstances and to see timestamps and request details. Use AWS Config when you need to know the configuration state of resources over time — for example, to find when a bucket became publicly readable or to see tag history on an EC2 instance. In many real-world scenarios you will use both: CloudTrail provides forensic detail about who performed actions, and Config provides the configuration outcome and a compliance signal. For automated governance, combine them: CloudTrail into CloudWatch Logs for real-time alerts and AWS Config Rules for continuous evaluation and remediation. A specific example: if a compliance requirement states that all EBS volumes must be encrypted, use Config with a managed or custom rule to continuously audit encryption; use CloudTrail only if you need to know who created or modified an unencrypted volume. A danger to avoid is assuming one service covers both needs — treating Config as a full audit log or CloudTrail as a compliance engine leads to blind spots. The practical question to close with is: for your top three governance needs, which service or combination provides the clearest answer?

Application
Which service answers which question?
Map common needs to CloudTrail, Config, or both for effective governance.
Who did it?

CloudTrail provides the identity, API call, and timestamp needed for forensic analysis.

What does it look like?

AWS Config shows the resource's configuration and history so you can assess drift and root causes.

Is it compliant?

Config Rules evaluate compliance continuously and can surface non-compliant resources for remediation.

fullNarratorScript:
In cloud operations, being able to answer who did what, and how resources changed, is essential for security and compliance. In this chapter you will learn the distinct but complementary roles of two AWS services: CloudTrail, which records A P I activity across your account, and AWS Config, which records what your resources look like and how they change over time. You will see practical configuration steps to enable CloudTrail across all regions, deliver logs to an S3 bucket and CloudWatch Logs, and create alerts for important events. You will also learn how AWS Config captures configuration items, evaluates resources against managed or custom Config Rules, and reports non-compliance so you can automate remediation. These capabilities together give you an audit trail for investigations and a continuous compliance posture for governance. As you work through the hands-on scenario, focus on the practical trade-offs: CloudTrail gives forensic detail about actions, while Config gives the history of resource state. By the end, you should be able to choose which service to use for a given governance goal and design a logging and compliance baseline that reduces manual review and speeds incident response. Which question would you ask first when designing an audit plan?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the fundamental differences between CloudTrail and AWS Config, and understand when to use each service. You will configure CloudTrail to capture A P I activity across all AWS regions, deliver logs to an S3 bucket, and forward events to CloudWatch Logs for real-time monitoring. You will also enable AWS Config to record resource configurations and history, add managed or custom Config Rules to continuously evaluate compliance, and interpret a resource's compliance state. These competencies matter because they let you investigate incidents, demonstrate compliance, and automate corrective actions. For example, you'll create a trail that writes to a logging bucket in a dedicated account so logs cannot be altered, and you'll add a Config Rule that flags public S3 buckets and required tags on EC2 instances. This combination reduces manual audits, speeds incident response, and helps satisfy regulatory requirements. Which of these objectives will you try first in your sandbox environment?

This second objectives slide focuses on practical outcomes you'll perform in the hands-on scenario. You will enable a trail that applies to all regions, create a new S3 bucket for logs, and forward CloudTrail events to CloudWatch Logs so you can build alarms for high-priority events like root user activity. You will also enable AWS Config to record all resources, create an S3 bucket for Config snapshots and an SNS topic for notifications, and add rules such as s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited and required-tags with a parameter for the Environment tag. These steps matter because they move governance from inspection to automation: alarms notify you quickly, and Config Rules continuously evaluate your environment. A common operational pattern is to put logs and Config history in a separate account and protect that S3 bucket to prevent tampering during investigations. When you practice these steps, think about the balance between visibility and cost, especially when enabling data events in CloudTrail. Which configuration will you test first in your sandbox?

Let's clarify the core difference between AWS CloudTrail and AWS Config using practical questions you might ask. If you need to know who called the A P I to create an EC2 instance, which A P I operation ran, and when it occurred, CloudTrail is the service that answers that question. CloudTrail records A P I calls made by users, roles, or AWS services, and delivers those events to S3 and optionally to CloudWatch Logs for real-time monitoring. By contrast, if you need to know whether an S3 bucket is currently publicly accessible or what its configuration was last week, AWS Config answers that. Config captures configuration items — snapshots of resource settings — and stores a history you can query. A useful mental model is: CloudTrail tells you what happened; Config tells you what things look like and how they changed. A common misconception is thinking Config replaces CloudTrail; it does not. They are complementary: CloudTrail helps with forensic timelines and who-did-what; Config helps you detect drift from desired configuration and assess compliance. For example, if an S3 bucket's policy changed and a public object appears, CloudTrail shows which A P I call modified the policy and who made it, while Config shows the resulting public configuration and flags the bucket as non-compliant if you have a rule for public-read. The takeaway is to design logging and compliance together: enable CloudTrail for events you care about and use Config Rules to continuously evaluate the resource state you must enforce. Which question will you ask first in your next incident review?

AWS CloudTrail is essentially an audit log for your AWS account. It records A P I calls and related events made by users, roles, or AWS services, creating a timeline of actions you can use for security analysis, troubleshooting, and compliance. Practically, enabling CloudTrail means you will receive event files in an S3 bucket and can optionally forward those events to CloudWatch Logs to build alerts. A best practice is to enable a multi-region trail so you capture events across all regions and to store logs in a dedicated, tightly controlled S3 bucket — ideally in a separate logging account — to reduce the risk of tampering during an incident. CloudTrail distinguishes management events and data events: management events capture control plane operations like creating or deleting resources, while data events capture resource-level operations such as S3 object A P I calls or Lambda invocation records. A common decision point is whether to enable data events, because they can be high volume and increase cost. You should choose data events selectively for critical resources where object-level visibility matters. For example, enabling S3 data events for a bucket that contains sensitive data helps detect unauthorized object reads. A misconception to avoid is relying on CloudTrail alone for compliance: CloudTrail shows actions, but it does not assess whether your resources are configured correctly—use Config for that. How would you choose which S3 buckets to include as data events in your account?

This lesson walks through the process of creating a CloudTrail trail that writes to an S3 logging bucket and to CloudWatch Logs so you can create alerts. Start by creating a new trail and select the option to apply it to all regions. When you create the trail, choose or create a dedicated S3 bucket for logs. Protect that bucket with restrictive ACLs and consider placing it in a separate logging account to reduce tampering risk. Next, enable the CloudWatch Logs integration and create a log group for the trail. With events streaming into CloudWatch Logs you can create a metric filter that looks for root user activity or other critical events, and then create an alarm that publishes to an SNS topic. The chapter provides a filter pattern you can use to detect root activity. A common pitfall is forgetting to enable management events or misunderstanding data events: management events are essential for control plane visibility, while data events are optional and should be enabled for high-value resources only. In practice, enable a baseline of management events for all resources, forward to CloudWatch Logs for rapid detection, and add data events selectively where needed. When you create the alarm, test by triggering a benign root-level event in a controlled environment and confirm the SNS notification. What specific event would you choose to validate your alarm without creating risk?

AWS Config continuously monitors and records configuration changes for supported AWS resources. Every time a supported resource changes, Config captures a Configuration Item — a snapshot of that resource's settings at a point in time. This recorded history lets you answer questions like what a security group's inbound rules looked like yesterday, or whether an EC2 instance's tag changed before a deployment failure. Config can be set to record all resources or only selected resource types; it delivers snapshots and a configuration history to an S3 bucket and sends notifications to an SNS topic. A practical benefit is troubleshooting: when an application breaks, use Config to find recent configuration changes that could explain the behavior. Importantly, Config is not an event log of who called an A P I; it records the resulting resource configuration. A common misconception is to rely on Config alone for auditing A P I activity — it will tell you that a configuration changed, but CloudTrail tells you who made the A P I call that caused it. When enabling Config, create an IAM role for Config if prompted, and plan a bucket for snapshots and history. The core insight is that Config gives you the state and history needed to detect drift and measure compliance over time. How would you use configuration history to accelerate a post-incident review?

AWS Config Rules let you evaluate whether resources meet your desired configuration. Rules can be managed (predefined) or custom. A managed rule example mentioned in the chapter is s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited, which flags S3 buckets that allow public read access. Another common managed rule is required-tags, which checks whether specific keys like Environment exist on resources such as EC2 instances. When you add a rule, Config continuously evaluates resources and marks them as compliant or non-compliant. For non-compliant resources you can trigger remediation, for example by invoking AWS Systems Manager Automation documents or other automated workflows. This moves governance from periodic audits to continuous enforcement. A practical implementation pattern is to align Config Rules with organizational policy and regulatory frameworks so compliance reporting is automated. Be mindful of rule scope and parameters: set required-tags with a Tag1Key parameter equal to Environment when that is your policy. A typical misconception is expecting immediate results; Config evaluations run on a schedule and may take a few minutes to appear. In practice, test rules in a non-production account and tune their scope to reduce noise. The closing question is: which rule would you enable first to reduce your organization's highest compliance risk?

AWS Config Rules evaluate resources continuously and report whether resources are compliant or non-compliant against the rule's desired state.
